| CR2, Satterthwaite df | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "t"))` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "df"), 1)` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "p"), 4)` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "r_formula"))` |

: One estimate under three kinds of inference: the reproduced specification, b = `r num(ref$b, 5)`, whose descriptive partial correlation is `r num(ref$r)` under every rule. Source: `data/display_inference.csv`. {#tbl-inference}

The last column shows why the curve plots the descriptive partial correlation and tests it separately: the conversion r = t / sqrt(t^2^ + df) recovers the partial correlation only from the conventional t and the residual df, and fed a clustered t with its smaller df it returns a larger number although the evidence is weaker, a trap that [the background page](background.qmd#sec-conversion) sets out.

## Admissible combinations {#admissibility}

Not every combination of options exists, and the browser lab and the workspace tell you when you have combined two that do not go together:

- **Published series ← predictor.** The unemployment series go with unemployment and the growth series with growth.
- **Predictor form ← predictor.** GDP growth takes negative values and enters raw only.
- **Imputed answers ← the standard settings.** The two imputation engines were run with raw unemployment in the World Bank series, all items and cells as interviewed, so they combine only with those settings.
- **Outcome family ← scoring rule.** The beta family needs a proportion strictly between 0 and 1: the share and the rate qualify, the count does not.
- **Off-curve options ← one at a time.** Each option off the curve was fitted against the specifications of the curve with every other decision on its curve options, so a combination of two off-curve options, such as a count under pooled OLS, was never fitted.

---

## Claim alignment {#the-claim-alignment-step}

Every outcome on the curve is a positive framing, for which the claim predicts a **negative** coefficient on unemployment, so for unemployment specifications the partial correlation needs no alignment: below zero is the direction of the claim. One flip remains. When the predictor is GDP growth, the claim predicts a **positive** coefficient on the positive framings, so the claim-aligned value multiplies b, t and r by −1 (the lab applies this for you), and after the flip below zero means the direction of the claim for every specification on the curve, whatever it measures.

The negative scales have their own curve, on which the alignment is reversed so that below zero is the direction of the other half of the first hypothesis, an increase in negative framing. Reversing the sign of r there is equivalent to reverse-coding the negative scale as 1 − y before fitting, which flips the sign of the coefficient and leaves its standard error, |t| and p-value untouched. Alignment changes the direction in which the evidence is stated and nothing about the evidence itself.

---

## Worked example

**Choice:** frame set `mpos`, scoring rule `share`, predictor `unemp`, adjustment `none`, sample `all`, whose average `none`, estimator `fe_twoway`; respondents who mention nothing `drop`, item set `all`, cell weighting `unweighted`, series `wb_nat`; form `raw`, family `gaussian`, inference by CR2 errors clustered by country with Satterthwaite df.

**Justification, by group.** The claim speaks of positive dimensions in the plural, which the composite scale captures more directly than the cosmopolitan scale alone, and the share is kept because the claim concerns how people frame the EU rather than how much they say about it. The comparison that the claim makes is that of a country with itself as its economy deteriorates, net of whatever all member states went through together in a year, which is what two-way fixed effects estimate; nothing in the claim restricts the countries or the years, and the claim is about countries, so every country-year counts once. Respondents who mention nothing are left out, following the code of the original study, because a person with no framing of the EU is not a person with zero positive framing, and the World Bank series is kept because it is the series on which the panel was built. The raw percentage is kept because the claim gives no warrant for a proportional effect, and the slope is tested with CR2 errors clustered by country and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, because the residuals of a country correlate from year to year and a few countries carry most of the variation.

A justification of this kind makes a specification defensible, because it connects each choice to the wording of the claim or to an argument about the data, according to the group to which the choice belongs.

---

## Justifying each decision {#what-each-decision-commits-you-to}

A decision can carry almost none of the variance on the curve and still decide whether *your* result clears p = 0.05, because significance is a property of one specification and variance is a property of the whole set. The rule for respondents who mention nothing carries `r pct(fk("noop"))` of the variance and changes the class of `r pct(fk("noop", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs; the predictor form carries `r pct(fk("pred_form"), 2)` and changes `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))`. Fix the question by fixing the four decisions about it that vary on the curve, leave the measurement decisions and the form free, and `r sum(questions$straddle)` of the `r nrow(questions)` questions still contain both a specification below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 and one that is not, which is why you fix your specification in the preregistration before you run it.
